content: {"findings": [{"file": "src/review_agents/context/modules.py", "line_start": 175, "line_end": 177, "severity": "important", "title": "Cache read outside a transaction, write not committed; assumes autocommit semantics not guaranteed", "why": "module_summaries executes INSERT OR REPLACE on `conn` without an explicit commit, and the same pattern is used in repo_layer.build_repo_layer for the layer cache. If the caller's connection is not in autocommit mode (connect()'s behavior is not shown here, and tests commit via closing()/migrate), the INSERTs may be rolled back when the connection closes. Even where autocommit holds, the cache write races with other builders: two workers can both miss the cache, both call the model, and both write — costing duplicate summary tokens. There is no transaction guarding read-then-write, so concurrent builds of the same module will double-spend the summary budget."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/context/repo_layer.py", "line_start": 128, "line_end": 144, "severity": "important", "title": "Layer cache and module cache are written but never committed, and the cache insert races the model call", "why": "build_repo_layer writes the conventions/tree row inside the same `conn` it later uses for module_summaries, but never commits. If the connection is rolled back (context manager without commit, or an exception later in the build), the expensive layer and summary caches are lost and rebuilt on every run — defeating the whole point of caching and repeatedly spending summary tokens. There is also no locking around the SELECT-then-INSERT, so concurrent builds of the same repo/tree each summarize every module before one wins the INSERT OR REPLACE."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/context/modules.py", "line_start": 35, "line_end": 42, "severity": "robustness", "title": "Every subdirectory under a split parent becomes its own model-summarised module, so module count is unbounded by file count", "why": "split_modules, for any directory over MAX_MODULE_FILES, emits the parent's own files as a module and then recurses into every child, and the module_summaries contract is 'no cap on how many' with each module invoking the model unless cached. In a repo with many small subdirectories under a big top-level tree (e.g. src/a, src/b, ... with a few files each), that is one model call per directory, not per 50 files. The advertised 'modules are directories of at most 50 files' is false for split parents, and the per-build token budget is the only backstop — which means a large repo degrades to stats for most modules on a cold cache and pays a burst of summary calls on every tree change that invalidates nothing (only modules changed are re-summarised, but a first build of a monorepo summarises hundreds of directories)."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/context/modules.py", "line_start": 155, "line_end": 160, "severity": "important", "title": "Summary cache is not written when the summary call succeeds but the outer transaction fails, and a failed summary is never retried", "why": "When summarize() raises a non-budget exception, the module keeps its stats and the exception is swallowed, but nothing is cached. On the next build the module is summarised again, so a persistently failing module (or a model outage) causes a fresh model call for every module on every build, burning budget that the budget-stop cannot see because BudgetExceededError is only raised from the meter. Combined with the no-commit issue above, this can mean repeated full-repo summarisation passes."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/context/markup.py", "line_start": 6, "line_end": 11, "severity": "important", "title": "Closing-tag regex misses the exact terminator forms the wrapper itself uses and adjacent variants", "why": "The wrapper emits `</untrusted>`. _CLOSING_TAG = r'</\\s*untrusted' matches `</untrusted` case-insensitively with optional whitespace, so the literal closing tag in content is defused. But it does not match `</untrusted >`, `< /untrusted>`, `</untrusted\\n>`, or an attacker-controlled source string, and it does not match a self-closing or attribute-bearing opening tag `</untrusted foo=...>` … actually the opening tag `<untrusted source=...>` is fine. However the `source` attribute is interpolated without escaping: untrusted('module:' + path, ...) where path comes from a directory name. A repo file path containing `"` or `>` (legal on POSIX) breaks out of the attribute and injects a closing tag or new attribute, so the data-block promise fails. Path is used unescaped in f'<untrusted source=\"{source}\">'."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/context/summarizer.py", "line_start": 17, "line_end": 24, "severity": "robustness", "title": "Summarizer returns raw model content with no length cap or content validation", "why": "A model summary is inserted verbatim into the cached JSON and then into the rendered module map. There is no truncation or sanity bound on reply.content. A prompt-injected or misbehaving model can return arbitrary text (including another closing tag, though untrusted() defuses that) of arbitrary length; because the summary is cached and the token budget only meters tokens, an oversized summary inflates every subsequent render's token estimate and context. No max-length check is applied before caching."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/context/git.py", "line_start": 56, "line_end": 66, "severity": "robustness", "title": "read_text does a linear scan of all files per call, making sample_module O(files × module files) and quadratic on large repos", "why": "read_text(path) calls next((f for f in self.files() ...)) which scans every file in the snapshot for each path. sample_module calls read_text for every file in a module (up to hundreds after the ordering), and convention reading calls it repeatedly. On a repo with tens of thousands of files this is quadratic and can dominate build time; the 30 s git timeout applies per git invocation so it does not bound the Python loop."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/context/git.py", "line_start": 59, "line_end": 64, "severity": "robustness", "title": "read_text uses the -l size from ls-tree but the actual blob may be larger; size check vs MAX_FILE_BYTES is on the cached tree size and can miss overflow", "why": "ls-tree -l gives the blob size at that commit, so this is accurate for the pinned commit; the real gap is that read_text only checks entry.size against MAX_FILE_BYTES but then cat-file reads the whole blob regardless — there is no upper bound handed to git, and a file at exactly MAX_FILE_BYTES still gets fully loaded and decoded. Combined with sample_module truncating to remaining*4 chars after full decode, memory peaks at full file size per read, which is bounded but the check is `>` not `>=` and allows a file of exactly the cap."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/context/modules.py", "line_start": 178, "line_end": 179, "severity": "important", "title": "Cache-hit read casts row['content'] but sqlite3.Row access may not be enabled, and json.loads on a missing 'summary' key raises", "why": "json.loads(row['content'])['summary'] assumes the stored content is always a dict with a 'summary' key. The layer cache and module cache share the `context_cache` table and are distinguished only by `layer='repo'` plus a cache_key prefix; but the module cache key is `module:...` while the layer key is `layer:<sha>`, and both use layer='repo'. A key collision is unlikely, but if the schema or content shape ever differs (e.g. an older SUMMARY_VERSION row with a different shape) the KeyError is not caught and aborts the entire build_repo_layer. Also, `row['content']` requires sqlite3.Row row_factory; if connect() does not set it, this raises TypeError. The tests rely on row['content'] working, so this is only a robustness concern if row_factory is not guaranteed."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/models.py", "line_start": 73, "line_end": 92, "severity": "robustness", "title": "review_usage/summary_usage open a fresh connection per call but with create=False; if the db has not been migrated the insert fails inside the model callback", "why": "Previously UsageMeter held db_path and could be constructed after migrate; now the record closure is created by the caller. If a caller builds review_usage(db_path, ...) before migrate() has run the new summary_usage table (old databases upgraded at startup but a code path that constructs the meter before the migration in the same process), the INSERT raises inside the LangChain callback thread. Errors in callbacks are logged and swallowed by LangChain, so usage is silently lost rather than crashing — a broken accounting contract. review_usage has the same risk against `usage`."}, {"file": "tests/test_db.py", "line_start": 60, "line_end": 64, "severity": "robustness", "title": "Test change masks a real migration concern: LATEST is computed at import time from _migrations(), so it does not detect duplicate versions", "why": "_migrations() imported and max()'d directly couples the test to a private function and computes LATEST at module import. If a future migration file is added with a version lower than the highest, max() silently skips it and the idempotency test still passes while migrate() may apply it out of order. Not a bug introduced in production code, but the test no longer verifies the specific expected version and cannot catch duplicate version numbers (max of a set with duplicates)."}, {"file": "src/review_agents/migrations/0002_summary_usage.sql", "line_start": 2, "line_end": 10, "severity": "robustness", "title": "summary_usage has no index on repo or created_at, so per-repo usage queries scan the whole table", "why": "The table will accumulate one row per module summary across many repos and builds. summary_usage(repo) writes rows with only a repo column and no index is created, so any usage rollup (per repo, per period) does a full table scan. Also created_at default format `%f` yields milliseconds, not the ISO second precision used elsewhere; mixing formats makes range queries in tests/rollups fragile."}]}
